ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The pistons $a$ and $b$, with cross-sectional areas $S$ and $3S$ respectively, are connected by a vertical light rod and enclose a certain mass of ideal gas within a vertically fixed cylinder. A mass $m$ is suspended below piston $a$, and the system is in a static state at the position shown, where the length of the upper gas column is $2L$ and the length of the lower gas column is $3L$. The external atmospheric pressure is constant at $p$, the thermodynamic temperature of the enclosed gas is $T_{1}=270\mathrm{K}$, the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is $g$, and the masses and thicknesses of the two pistons are negligible, as is all friction.

1. What is the pressure \( p_{1} \) of the enclosed gas?
2. Now, the enclosed gas is slowly heated until the piston $b$ rises to a height of $L$. What is the thermodynamic temperature $T_{2}$ of the enclosed gas at this point?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a vertically fixed stepped cylinder, with a larger piston b above and a smaller piston a below; the cross-sectional area of piston b is 3S, and the cross-sectional area of piston a is S. The two pistons are connected by a vertical light rod. An object of mass m is suspended below piston a. The figure marks the length of the upper gas column as 2L and the length of the lower gas column as 3L, and the gas is enclosed between the two pistons. Reasoning: Regard piston a, piston b, the light rod, and the suspended object m as one whole. The upper piston b is subjected to the upward pressure p1·3S from the gas and the downward pressure p0·3S from the atmosphere; the lower piston a is subjected to the downward pressure p1·S from the gas and the upward pressure p0·S from the atmosphere; the suspended object provides the downward gravity mg. Therefore the resultant force of the gas on the whole is upward p1(3S-S), and the resultant force of the atmosphere on the whole is downward p0(3S-S). Static equilibrium gives (p1-p0)(3S-S)=mg, that is, p1=p0+mg/(2S). If in the problem the atmospheric pressure is denoted as p, then the same formula is written as p1=p+mg/(2S). During the slow heating process, the external load, piston areas, and geometric constraints do not change, so the gas pressure remains at the above constant value, and it is an isobaric process. The initial-state volume is read from the two sections of gas columns in the figure: V1=3S·2L+S·3L=6SL+3SL=9SL. When piston b rises by L, the light rod makes piston a also rise by L; thus the length of the upper gas column changes from 2L to 3L, and the length of the lower gas column changes from 3L to 2L. The final-state volume is V2=3S·3L+S·2L=9SL+2SL=11SL. An ideal gas at constant pressure satisfies T2/T1=V2/V1, therefore T2=270×11/9=330 K.
